name: Cocama
confidence_why: Vallejos Yopán's 2010 reference grammar gives fixed penultimate stress as the general rule, and the earlier first-hand descriptions by Faust & Pike (1959) and Faust (1972) agree for vowel-final words while adding that words ending in -n, the only possible final consonant, take final stress, a refinement of the weight condition rather than a different system.
catalog_quote: In KK, word stress has delimitative functions. In general, stress is fixed and occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word. Therefore, stress constitutes the basic criterion to identify word boundaries in KK.

new_statements.quote: Con muy pocas excepciones, las palabras cocamas terminadas en vocal se acentúan en la penúltima sílaba: tucáca "a mi casa". Las palabras que terminan en n (la n es la única consonante que puede ser final de palabra) llevan el acento en la última sílaba: yanucatán "tela". Los acentos de cada palabra se pierden o se debilitan dentro de la oración cargándose el acento fuerte en la penúltima sílaba de la oración si la palabra termina en vocal; y en la última sílaba, si termina en n: Tucaca tútsu "me voy a mi casa". [p. 148] — p. 12 fn. 3: Cuando se agrega el sufijo -ca- a un pronombre de una sílaba, el acento cae en -ca-.
new_statements.translation: With very few exceptions, Cocama words ending in a vowel are stressed on the penultimate syllable: tucáca 'to my house'. Words ending in n (n is the only consonant that can be word-final) carry the stress on the last syllable: yanucatán 'cloth'. The stresses of the individual words are lost or weakened within the sentence, the strong stress falling on the penultimate syllable of the sentence if the word ends in a vowel, and on the last syllable if it ends in n: Tucaca tútsu 'I am going to my house'. — fn. 3 p. 12: When the suffix -ca- is added to a monosyllabic pronoun, the stress falls on -ca-.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) gives plain penultimate stress at every word length. Faust agrees for vowel-final words (the majority) but adds that n-final words are stressed on the ultima, which the catalog's all-penult rule does not capture; compatible if the catalog's penult is read as the default for open final syllables.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress the penult of vowel-final words; stress the ultima of words ending in n (the only possible final consonant), i.e. a closed final syllable attracts stress, otherwise penultimate. Word stresses weaken inside the sentence, where the phrase-final word keeps the strong stress on the same syllable (penult if vowel-final, ultima if n-final).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Con muy pocas excepciones' (very few exceptions, not enumerated); exercises mark the stressed syllable only where the rules are not met; monosyllabic pronoun + -ca- is stressed on -ca- (p. 12 fn. 3). Note: the copy downloaded is the 2008 3rd edition (Spanish version by Ezequiel Romero, revised by Walter del Águila and Irma Inugay), not the 1978 printing; content of the grammar is the same work.
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe Peruvian Cocama (Loreto, SIL Peru data, 1950s-70s); Vallejos & Koops use the current name Kukama-Kukamiria for the same language (coca1259). new_statements.quote: Con muy pocas excepciones, las palabras cocamas que terminan en vocal llevan el acento en la penúltima sílaba: tucáca "a mi casa". Las palabras terminadas en la consonante n llevan el acento en la última sílaba: *yucún "eso". (La n es la única consonante que aparece como final en cocama.) En una oración, los acentos de cada palabra a menudo se pierden o se moderan. Se acentúa la penúltima sílaba de la oración si termina en vocal: Tucaca tútsu. "Voy a mi casa". En los ejercicios, se marcará la sílaba tónica con un acento, solamente en los casos en que no se cumplan estas reglas. [p. 11]
new_statements.translation: With very few exceptions, Cocama words that end in a vowel carry the stress on the penultimate syllable: tucáca 'to my house'. Words ending in the consonant n carry the stress on the last syllable: *yucún 'that'. (n is the only consonant that occurs word-finally in Cocama.) In a sentence, the stresses of the individual words are often lost or moderated. The penultimate syllable of the sentence is stressed if it ends in a vowel: Tucaca tútsu 'I am going to my house'. In the exercises the stressed syllable will be marked with an accent only in the cases where these rules are not met.

new_statements.quote: This study provides a phonetically grounded, usage-based account of word-level prosody in Kukama-Kukamiria (KK, Tupian), a language of the Peruvian Amazon. KK exhibits two types of prosodic prominence at the word level: primary stress on the penultimate syllable and secondary stress on the initial syllable. Importantly, both are blind to the morphosyntactic composition of the word. In addition, KK displays a pervasive pattern of unstressed vowel reduction and deletion that happen across-the-board, targeting any vowel that carries neither primary nor secondary stress. Yet deletion disproportionately affects post-tonic vowels. Thus, the KK pattern of unstressed vowel reduction is governed by the vowels’ position in the prosodic structure of the word.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the sources opened. The only tension is with the catalog's StressTyp2 record, which gives plain penultimate stress at every length: Faust's grammar (1972/1978, read in the 2008 3rd edition, pp. 11 and 148) gives penult for vowel-final words but ultima for words ending in n, the only possible final consonant, so the placement is conditioned by a closed final syllable rather than being uniformly penultimate., sec. 3 'Stress', pp. 20-23) says the same, adds that the future morpheme -a makes primary-stress placement minimally contrastive (tata vs ta'ta), and describes non-contrastive alternating secondary stress counting leftward from the primary; Faust's grammar says nothing on secondary stress. The Vallejos & Koops 2018 instrumental study could not be opened. Penultimate primary stress is common ground between the catalog (StressTyp2: penultimate stress), Faust 1972/2008 (the default for vowel-final words), the held Vallejos 2010 dissertation (§3.3.1 p. 119, the catalog quote) and the Vallejos & Koops 2018 abstract. The one substantive disagreement is over n-final words: Faust (p. 11, p. 148) says words ending in n, the only permitted final consonant, are stressed on the final syllable, a closure-sensitive right-edge rule, which is why the Faust statements held by the project are coded weight-sensitive rather than strict penult; Vallejos 2010 (§3.3.2 p. 121) rejects the consonant-final = final-stress analysis and attributes word-final stress to a closed s…

The Kokama words ending in /y/ are all monossilabics. [Chart 7, p. 60] ... In Kokama, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a phonological word if the last syllable is open, otherwise stress falls on the last syllable. [p. 276] ... Stress is nondistinctive in Kokama. Generally, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a phonological word. However, in words ending in /w/, /y/ or /n/, stress falls on the final syllable. Kokama has a small number of particles with final stress. An example of this is ikwa 'recent past'. [p. 315]

sources.citation: Vallejos, Rosa & Christian Koops. 2018. Word-level prosody in Kukama-Kukamiria: The interplay of stress and vowel reduction. Paper presented at AMAZONICAS VII, Baños, Ecuador, 28 May-1 June 2018 (slides).
sources.quote: This study provides a phonetically grounded, usage-based account of word-level prosody in Kukama-Kukamiria (KK, Tupian), a language of the Peruvian Amazon. KK exhibits two types of prosodic prominence at the word level: primary stress on the penultimate syllable and secondary stress on the initial syllable. Importantly, both are blind to the morphosyntactic composition of the word. In addition, KK displays a pervasive pattern of unstressed vowel reduction and deletion that happen across-the-board, targeting any vowel that carries neither primary nor secondary stress. Yet deletion disproportionately affects post-tonic vowels. Thus, the KK pattern of unstressed vowel reduction is governed by the vowels’ position in the prosodic structure of the word.

sources.quote: En la lengua kukama-kukamiria el acento es fijo, es asignado a la segunda sílaba contando desde la última. Su función es estrictamente delimitativa con lo cual se constituye en uno de los principales criterios para la identificación de límites entre palabras. [p. 112] ... En estos casos es posible identificar un acento primario (`), en la penúltima sílaba, y uno secundario (``), nuevamente en la penúltima sílaba contando desde la sílaba con acento primario con lo cual el patrón base no varía. ja.``wa.ra.`pa.na "tigre negro"; ka.ri.``ka.ri.`ta.ka "saltar en un pie"; i.``min.tsa.`ra.ka "conversar" [p. 113] ... Estamos postulando que en esta lengua existe un grupo de morfemas que tienen el acento como parte de su estructura. [p. 113] ... Los sufijos en mención mantienen su acento siempre y cuando sean terminales, es decir, si en ellos finaliza la palabra. Si esta palabra es sufijada nuevamente, se recupera el patrón acentual de la lengua y por consiguiente la sílaba acentuada vuelve a ser la penúltima. [p. 114]

tone.quote: Generally, the stress in both Omagua and Kokama falls on the penultimate syllable, e.g. Kokama [pa.ˈna.ɾa] ‘banana’, Omagua [ta.ˈpa.ka] ‘piranha sp.’. The exception to this in Kokama is when a stress-bearing morpheme is attached, in which case the stress becomes final: /panaɾa-pan/ [pa.na.ɾa.ˈpan] ‘banana-der’ (Vallejos, 2010:62-66). [p. 17:] McWhorter (1998, 2001) identifies three features which will identify a language as a creole. These are (1) minimal use of inflection, (2) lack of tone, (3) semantically regular derivation.
